examShortTricks: Trick 1: Unit questions test argument evaluation — find the writer's CLAIM, the EVIDENCE and the ASSUMPTION; a missing-evidence comment earns the analysis mark.
Trick 2: For 'do you agree?' items, use the 3-step reply: concede one point, refute with evidence, restate your position.
practiceQuestions: Q. What assumption does the writer's argument rest on? (2 marks) — identify the unstated premise and explain how the claim depends on it.
Q. Give one counter-argument to the writer's claim. (2 marks) — state it fairly, then say why it is weaker.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Family questions in this unit revolve around generational change — contrast the text's family values with modern urban life in one paragraph.
Trick 2: Character questions: show the character through DIALOGUE, then interpret the relationship dynamic it reveals.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does the text portray the bond between generations? (2 marks) — affection mixed with duty and misunderstanding; cite one exchange.
Q. Should elderly parents live with their children? (2 marks) — balanced answer: companionship and care vs independence; end with your view.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Sports passages are stat-heavy — mark numbers, names and superlatives; factual questions target them directly.
Trick 2: Essay questions on sports: pick the values angle (discipline, teamwork, health) and argue with one real example, not a list.
practiceQuestions: Q. What values does playing sport build? (2 marks) — discipline and teamwork; one sentence each with an example.
Q. Why should schools invest in sports? (2 marks) — physical health plus concentration and character; link to academics.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Technology questions demand balance: name TWO benefits and TWO harms, then take a stance — the 'both faces' pattern is the top band.
Trick 2: Vocabulary matters: artificial intelligence, digital divide, screen time — use the unit's own terms in your answers.
practiceQuestions: Q. How has technology changed education? (2 marks) — access to resources and interactive learning; mention the digital divide as a caution.
Q. Is social media more harmful than helpful? (2 marks) — connectivity vs addiction/misinformation; conclude with your stance.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Education questions reward the purpose debate: knowledge vs grades vs character — frame your answer around what education is FOR.
Trick 2: Quote one concrete Nepali context point (exam-oriented rote learning, access gaps) — local grounding lifts the answer.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is the true aim of education? (2 marks) — developing thinking and character, not merely certificates; support with one example.
Q. How can exam-oriented learning be improved? (2 marks) — project work and critical questioning; continuous assessment.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Economic passages use cause-effect chains (inflation → prices → demand) — map the chain before answering comprehension questions.
Trick 2: 'Money and happiness' essays: state what money CAN buy (security) and cannot (meaning), then conclude — the two-column frame wins.
practiceQuestions: Q. Can money buy happiness? (2 marks) — money secures basics and reduces stress, but relationships and purpose matter more; conclude clearly.
Q. Why do people save money? (1 mark) — security against emergencies and future goals.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Name the humour device precisely: irony, pun, hyperbole, situational comedy — precision of device + the quoted instance is the full-mark pair.
Trick 2: 'Why is this funny?' answers must explain the INCONGRUITY (what we expected vs what happened) — expectation violation is the theory to cite.
practiceQuestions: Q. What makes the situation in the text humorous? (2 marks) — the gap between expectation and outcome; cite the moment.
Q. Identify one example of irony in the text. (2 marks) — quote the line and explain the intended vs actual meaning.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Culture questions expect the visible/invisible split: artefacts and festivals vs values and worldview — answer with one of each.
Trick 2: For culture-change questions, argue preservation THROUGH change (adaptation) rather than freezing culture — the nuanced stance scores.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does culture shape identity? (2 marks) — language, rituals and values give belonging; one example.
Q. Should traditions change with time? (2 marks) — yes, adapt their core values to new contexts; keep the meaning, update the form.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Environment questions: pair every PROBLEM with a SOLUTION — imbalance (all problems, no fixes) loses the band.
Trick 2: Use Nepal anchors: hydropower vs deforestation, plastic bans, community forestry — one local example per answer.
practiceQuestions: Q. Suggest two ways students can protect the environment. (2 marks) — reduce/reuse plastic and plant or protect trees; be specific.
Q. What is climate change doing to Nepal? (2 marks) — glacier melt and erratic rainfall affecting farming and hydropower.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Career questions test FORMAL WRITING: cover letter and CV conventions — follow the fixed format; content must match the advertised post.
Trick 2: Interview answers use the STAR frame: Situation, Task, Action, Result — one compact STAR example beats vague claims.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a cover letter for a teaching vacancy. (4 marks) — format, post and source, two matching qualifications, availability.
Q. How should you answer 'tell me about yourself' in an interview? (2 marks) — brief education, relevant skills, one achievement — under a minute.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: 'Describe your hobby' answers need SPECIFICS: when you started, what you actually do, one skill gained — concrete detail is the band marker.
Trick 2: Argue the value line: hobbies build skills and mental health — connect one hobby to one benefit, not a generic list.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why are hobbies important for students? (2 marks) — stress relief and skill-building; one concrete example.
Q. Describe a hobby of yours and what it has taught you. (3 marks) — specific activity, routine, one lesson learned.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Animal texts often argue ethics — organise answers as welfare facts (sentience, suffering) + human duty + one practice to change.
Trick 2: Comprehension questions target behaviour details (habitat, diet, instinct) — underline them during reading.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why should humans protect animal habitats? (2 marks) — biodiversity and ecosystem balance; human survival depends on it.
Q. Is keeping animals in zoos justified? (2 marks) — conservation and education vs captivity stress; end with conditions that justify it.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: History passages test chronology — build a quick timeline while reading; sequence questions then answer themselves.
Trick 2: 'Lessons from history' essays: pick ONE event, extract ONE principle (e.g. unpreparedness invites invasion), apply it to today.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why should we study history? (2 marks) — it explains present institutions and prevents repeating mistakes; one example.
Q. What can a historical event teach today's society? (2 marks) — name the event, the principle, the modern application.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Rights answers need the framework: UDHR 1948 → constitutional rights → enforcement gap — the three-layer structure is the mark.
Trick 2: For violation questions, name the right, the violator, the victim and the remedy — four slots, four marks.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name three fundamental rights in Nepal's constitution. (1 mark) — right to equality, education, freedom of expression (any three).
Q. How can human rights be protected in practice? (2 marks) — independent courts and free media; awareness and reporting.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Leisure questions contrast ACTIVE (sports, reading) vs PASSIVE (scrolling, TV) leisure — argue for active with one health or skill point.
Trick 2: 'Screen time' essays: acknowledge benefits, then set the cost (sleep, attention), then propose limits — the three-move structure.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does leisure benefit a working person? (2 marks) — recovery from stress and renewed creativity; one example.
Q. Is too much entertainment harmful? (2 marks) — passive excess costs sleep and study time; moderation and active hobbies as the answer.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Fantasy analysis: state the world's RULES (what magic can and cannot do) — internal logic is what makes fantasy coherent and is the analysis mark.
Trick 2: Allegory question: fantasy often mirrors reality (power, fear, hope) — name the real-world parallel of one fantasy element.
practiceQuestions: Q. What rules govern the imaginary world in the text? (2 marks) — list the limits of magic or the setting's laws; show how the plot respects them.
Q. What real-world issue might the fantasy reflect? (2 marks) — map one element (monster, quest) to a human problem.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: War texts demand TONE + EVIDENCE: label the tone (bitter, elegiac, patriotic) and quote the words that prove it — tone without evidence scores half.
Trick 2: Peace-building answers: name levels (personal forgiveness, social justice, international diplomacy) — the three levels show analytical depth.
practiceQuestions: Q. What tone does the writer adopt towards war? (2 marks) — name it and quote one phrase as evidence.
Q. How can lasting peace be achieved? (2 marks) — justice and reconciliation at social level plus diplomacy between states.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Music questions: link form to feeling — rhythm/melody create mood; state the mood first, then the musical cause.
Trick 2: 'Music is universal' essays: one shared-emotion argument + one cultural-specificity argument, then synthesis.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is music called a universal language? (2 marks) — it expresses emotion across cultures without words; give one example.
Q. How does music influence mood? (2 marks) — tempo and mode affect arousal and feeling; calm vs energetic examples.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Migration answers have three faces: cause (poverty, conflict), experience (displacement, identity), effect (remittances, brain drain) — cover all three.
Trick 2: Nepal context: remittance economy vs family separation — one paragraph on each side shows balance.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why do people migrate abroad? (2 marks) — employment and education; conflict as a push factor.
Q. What are the effects of migration on Nepal? (2 marks) — remittances support the economy; families separate and talent drains.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Political texts mix fact and persuasion — tag each sentence as fact or opinion while reading; stance questions then answer themselves.
Trick 2: 'Power and responsibility' essays: definition → corruption risk → accountability mechanisms → hopeful close; four moves, four marks.
practiceQuestions: Q. How should power be used responsibly? (2 marks) — transparency and service to the public; one institutional safeguard.
Q. Why does absolute power corrupt? (2 marks) — no checks breed impunity; give one historical or modern example.
